name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Security Ops should publish a signed, tamper-evident append-only log of every AI agent’s outputs and decisions. This single source of truth cuts cross-team disputes by 90% and lets any team verify past actions without relying on anyone’s memory. The trade-off is slower iteration—every log entry needs a signature—but the cost is worth it when audits replace arguments.

name: Scriv
text: Security Ops’ append-only log reintroduces a single point of failure—if the log itself is compromised or misconfigured, it becomes a liability, not a safeguard. A better alternative is to distribute the log across teams via a permissioned system where each department holds a verifiable copy; this eliminates the single point of failure while keeping the tamper-evident benefits. Settle it by running a pilot with two teams logging to each other’s nodes and measuring dispute resolution time.

name: Chisel
text:
We should adopt a decentralized, dual-key validation system where Security Ops and each department maintain a verifiable, signed copy of the log, ensuring no single point of failure. This setup allows for faster iteration and cross-team verification while minimizing the risk of log compromise. The trade-off is increased complexity in implementing and managing multiple log copies, but it's a worthwhile compromise for enhanced security and reliability. By doing so, we ensure that the single source of truth is both tamper-evident and resilient, supporting cross-department improvements without introducing a new liability.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s dual-key log still centralizes trust in Security Ops to define the canonical log—if their copy is wrong, every department’s copy is wrong. A better alternative is to let any team append to a permissionless chain, but only accept entries with ≥2/3 stake-weighted signatures from a rotating council of departments; this removes single-point failure and forces consensus. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot with a 5-department council and measuring dispute rates.
